Incorrect_Code:
if x = 5:
    print("five")
Underlying_Misconception: Confuses assignment (`=`, which stores a value) with equality comparison (`==`, which asks a question and produces a boolean). The learner carries over the "equals" sign from math, where it covers both meanings.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is this line asking Python a question or giving it an order?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A single = stores a value in a variable. A double == compares two values and gives back True or False. An if condition needs the comparison.
Resolution_Question: Write an if statement that prints "perfect" when score is equal to 100.

Incorrect_Code:
for i in range(len(a) + 1):
    print(a[i])
Underlying_Misconception: Misunderstands zero-based indexing. A list of length n has valid indices 0 to n-1, so the learner treats the length as the last index (an off-by-one error that raises IndexError).
Hint_L1_Socratic: If the list a has 5 items, what is the index of the last one, and what does range(len(a) + 1) produce?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Indexes start at 0, so a list of length n has valid indexes 0 to n-1. range(n) already stops at n-1, so adding 1 goes one step past the end.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Remove the `+ 1` so the loop uses `range(len(a))`.
Resolution_Question: Which index do you use to get the last item of a list named data with 8 items, and how can you get it without counting?

Underlying_Misconception: Believes default arguments are re-evaluated on every call. They are evaluated once, at function definition time, so a mutable default is shared across all calls.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does the default list get created every time you call the function, or only once?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Default values are evaluated once, when the def line runs. A mutable default like [] is then shared by every call that does not pass its own list.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Set the default to `lst=None`, then add `if lst is None: lst = []` as the first line of the body.
Resolution_Question: Rewrite `def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):` so each call without a list starts with a fresh empty list.

Underlying_Misconception: Conflates displaying a value (`print`, a side effect to the screen) with handing a value back to the caller (`return`). The learner assumes anything shown on screen is also available to the program.
Hint_L1_Socratic: After add(2, 3) runs, what does the variable r actually contain?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: print shows text on the screen but gives nothing back to the program. return hands a value to the caller so it can be stored or reused.
Resolution_Question: Write a function square(x) that returns the square of x, then store the result of square(4) in a variable.

Incorrect_Code:
age = input("Age: ")
print(age + 1)
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `input()` returns a number when the user types digits. It always returns a string, and the learner doesn't track data types as distinct from how values look when printed.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What type of data does input() give you, even if the user types 25?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: input() always returns a string. Adding an int to a string is not allowed, so the text must be converted to a number first.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Wrap the call in int(): `age = int(input("Age: "))`.
Resolution_Question: Ask the user for two numbers with input() and print their sum.

Correct_Code: nums = [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes the loop iterates over a frozen snapshot of the list. Iteration uses a live index into the collection, so removing items shifts elements and causes some to be skipped.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When you remove an item from a list during a loop, what happens to the position of the items after it?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A for loop walks through the list by position. Removing an item shifts later items left, so the loop jumps over the one that moved into the gap.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Build a new list instead: `nums = [n for n in nums if n % 2 != 0]`.
Resolution_Question: Using a list comprehension, keep only the words longer than 3 letters from words = ["a", "tree", "to", "house"].

Incorrect_Code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a
b.append(4)  # a also changed
Correct_Code:
a = [1, 2, 3]
b = a.copy()
b.append(4)  # a unchanged
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks assignment copies the data, as if variables were boxes holding values. Variables are names bound to objects, so `b = a` creates a second name for the same list (aliasing).
Hint_L1_Socratic: After b = a, how many lists exist in memory?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Assignment does not copy data. It gives the same object a second name, so a change made through b is visible through a.
Resolution_Question: Make a copy of scores = [1, 2, 3] called backup, add 4 to backup only, and show that scores is unchanged.

Incorrect_Code:
if answer is "yes":
    proceed()
Underlying_Misconception: Confuses object identity (`is`, same object in memory) with value equality (`==`). Code may appear to work for some strings because of interning and then fail unpredictably.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What is the difference between asking whether two things are the same object and asking whether they have the same value?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: `is` tests identity (same object in memory). `==` tests equality (same value). Strings with equal text are not guaranteed to be the same object.
Resolution_Question: Write a condition that checks whether the string command is equal to "quit".

Incorrect_Code:
name = "ada"
print(name.upper)
Underlying_Misconception: Doesn't distinguish referring to a function (the object itself) from calling it (executing it). The learner treats `.upper` as a property or the result rather than as a callable.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does name.upper give you the uppercase text, or something else?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A method name without parentheses refers to the method itself. Parentheses are what actually run it and produce a result.
Resolution_Question: Print the length of the string "python" using a method or function call written correctly.

Incorrect_Code:
s = "hello"
s[0] = "H"
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes strings are mutable, like a row of editable characters. Strings are immutable, so "changing" one means building a new string and rebinding the name.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Can you change one character inside a string the way you change one item in a list?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Strings are immutable. You cannot edit them in place, but you can build a new string and assign it to the same name.
Resolution_Question: Turn s = "cat" into "hat" without using s[0] = ...

Incorrect_Code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
nums = nums.sort()  # nums is None
Underlying_Misconception: Expects every method to return the transformed result. In-place mutating methods return `None` by convention, and the learner doesn't distinguish "modify this object" from "produce a new object."
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does nums.sort() return, and what happens when you assign that to nums?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Methods that change an object in place, like sort(), return None. The sorted list is stored in the original object, not returned.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Call `nums.sort()` on its own line, or use `nums = sorted(nums)`.
Resolution_Question: Sort names = ["Zoe", "Al", "Max"] in two ways: once in place and once producing a new list.

Incorrect_Code:
count = 0
def inc():
    count += 1
inc()  # UnboundLocalError
Correct_Code:
count = 0
def inc():
    global count
    count += 1
# better: def inc(c): return c + 1
Underlying_Misconception: Believes a function can freely read and modify variables from the enclosing scope. Assigning inside a function makes the name local, and the learner lacks a model of scope and namespaces.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Inside inc(), does Python treat count as the global one or as a new variable?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local to that function. To change the outer variable you must say so with global, or better, pass the value in and return the new one.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `global count` as the first line inside inc(), or change it to `def inc(c): return c + 1`.
Resolution_Question: Write a function that increases a global counter called visits by 1 each time it is called.

Underlying_Misconception: Doesn't realize `return` immediately terminates the function, including any loop. The learner views indentation as visual grouping rather than as defining control-flow structure.
Hint_L1_Socratic: On the first pass through the loop, which line runs after s += n?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: return ends the function immediately, including any loop. Its indentation decides whether it runs on every pass or once at the end.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Unindent `return s` so it lines up with `for`.
Resolution_Question: Write a function that returns the product of all numbers in a list.

Incorrect_Code:
if color == "red" or "blue":
    print("warm or cool")
Correct_Code:
if color in ("red", "blue"):
    print("warm or cool")
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes Python parses code like natural language ("color is red or blue"). Python evaluates `color == "red"` and `"blue"` as separate expressions, and a non-empty string is always truthy, so the condition is always true.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does Python evaluate separately in `color == "red" or "blue"`, and is "blue" true or false on its own?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Python does not read this like English. It checks `color == "red"` and then `"blue"` as two expressions, and a non-empty string is always truthy.
Resolution_Question: Write a condition that is True when day is "Sat" or "Sun".

Incorrect_Code:
grid = [[0] * 3] * 3
grid[0][0] = 1  # all rows change
Correct_Code:
grid = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]
grid[0][0] = 1  # only row 0 changes
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks `*` duplicates the inner list into independent copies. It repeats references to the same inner list, so this is the aliasing misconception (see ID 7) showing up in a nested data structure.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many separate inner lists does [[0] * 3] * 3 really create?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: The * operator repeats references to the same inner list. All three rows are the same object, so changing one changes all.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Build each row separately: `grid = [[0] * 3 for _ in range(3)]`.
Resolution_Question: Create a 4 x 2 grid of zeros where changing the first row does not change the others.

Underlying_Misconception: Believes the loop condition changes on its own, as if `i < 5` were a countdown. A `while` loop only re-checks the condition, so something in the body must change the state, otherwise it runs forever.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What inside this loop ever makes `i < 5` become False?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A while loop only re-checks its condition. Something in the body must change the variable, otherwise the loop never ends.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `i += 1` as the last line inside the loop.
Resolution_Question: Write a while loop that counts down from 10 to 1 and prints each number.

Incorrect_Code:
d = {"a": 1}
print(d["b"])  # KeyError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes a missing key quietly gives an empty or `None` value, like a blank spreadsheet cell. Subscript access on a dict raises `KeyError`, so absence must be handled with `in`, `.get()`, or `try/except`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does Python do when you ask a dict for a key it does not have?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Square brackets raise KeyError for a missing key. .get(key, default) returns the default instead of failing.
Resolution_Question: Safely read the key "age" from the dict user and use 0 if it is missing.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks looping over a dict yields key-value pairs. Iterating a dict yields only its keys, so unpacking two names from a string key fails. `.items()` is needed for pairs.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When you loop over a dict directly, what does each pass give you?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Looping over a dict yields only its keys. To get key and value together, use the .items() view.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Change `for k, v in d:` to `for k, v in d.items():`.
Resolution_Question: Print every name and score from scores = {"Ana": 90, "Raj": 85} in the form "Ana: 90".

Underlying_Misconception: Assumes a key starts at 0 the first time it is used. `+=` reads the existing value first, and a new key has none. The learner doesn't separate creating an entry from updating one.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does counts[w] return the very first time a word appears?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: += first reads the current value. A new key has no value yet, so the read fails. You must create the entry before updating it.
Resolution_Question: Count how many times each letter appears in the string "banana" using a dict.

Incorrect_Code: d = {[1, 2]: "point"}  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Believes any object can be a dict key. Keys must be hashable (immutable), because the dict locates entries by hash value, and a mutable list could change after insertion and become unfindable.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Why might Python refuse a list as a dict key?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Dict keys must be hashable, which means immutable. A list can change after being stored, so Python would lose track of where it was put.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use a tuple as the key: `{(1, 2): "point"}`.
Resolution_Question: Store the value "home" for the location 12.5, 77.6 in a dict, using a valid key.

Incorrect_Code:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])  # [2, 2, 2]
Correct_Code:
funcs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])  # [0, 1, 2]
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks a function captures the value of an outer variable when it is created. It captures the variable itself and looks it up when called (late binding), by which time the loop has finished.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When does each lambda look up the value of i: when it is created or when it is called?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Functions look up outer variables at call time (late binding). By then the loop has finished, so every lambda sees the last value of i.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Bind the current value with a default argument: `lambda i=i: i`.
Resolution_Question: Create a list of three functions where the first returns 10, the second 20 and the third 30, using a loop.

Incorrect_Code:
def make():
    result = 10
make()
print(result)  # NameError
Correct_Code:
def make():
    result = 10
    return result
result = make()
print(result)
Underlying_Misconception: Believes variables created inside a function persist after it ends. Local names exist only during the call, so data must leave the function through `return`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Where does the variable result exist after make() has finished running?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Variables created inside a function disappear when it ends. To get data out of a function, you return it and store it in the caller.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `return result` inside make() and write `result = make()` outside.
Resolution_Question: Write a function that computes the area of a rectangle and lets the caller print it.

Incorrect_Code:
list = [1, 2, 3]
words = list("abc")  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Treats names like `list`, `sum`, or `str` as reserved the way keywords are. Assigning to them creates a variable that shadows the built-in in the current scope, hiding the original.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does the name list refer to after you write list = [1, 2, 3]?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Built-in names like list, str and sum are ordinary names, not reserved words. Assigning to them hides the original in your code.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Rename the variable to something else, such as `items`.
Resolution_Question: Explain why `sum = 10` followed by `sum([1, 2])` fails, and rename the variable to fix it.

Incorrect_Code: [x for x in nums if x > 0 else 0]  # SyntaxError
Correct_Code: [x if x > 0 else 0 for x in nums]
Underlying_Misconception: Confuses the two roles of a condition. A trailing `if` filters items out, while `x if cond else y` is an expression that transforms every item, so it must go before the `for`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does the if in this comprehension decide which items to keep, or what value each item becomes?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A trailing if only filters items and cannot have an else. A value choice with else is an expression and goes before the for.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Move the condition to the front: `[x if x > 0 else 0 for x in nums]`.
Resolution_Question: Write a comprehension that replaces every negative number in nums with 0 and leaves others unchanged.

Incorrect_Code: flat = [x for x in row for row in matrix]
Correct_Code: flat = [x for row in matrix for x in row]
Underlying_Misconception: Reads the comprehension's nested `for` clauses in the wrong order. They follow the same order as nested loops written out normally (outer loop first), but the learner reads them as natural-language phrasing.
Hint_L1_Socratic: If you wrote the same thing with two normal nested for loops, which loop would be on the first line?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Nested for clauses in a comprehension appear in the same order as the nested loops: outer loop first, then inner loop.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Reorder to `[x for row in matrix for x in row]`.
Resolution_Question: Flatten [[1, 2], [3], [4, 5]] into one list using a single comprehension.

Incorrect_Code:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
[n * 2 for n in nums]
print(nums)  # [1, 2, 3]
Correct_Code:
nums = [1, 2, 3]
nums = [n * 2 for n in nums]
print(nums)  # [2, 4, 6]
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks a list comprehension transforms the original list in place, like a loop with side effects. It builds and returns a new list, which is lost unless assigned to a name.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What happens to the new list that the comprehension builds?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A comprehension creates a new list and does not change the original. If you do not assign the result to a name, it is thrown away.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Assign the result: `nums = [n * 2 for n in nums]`.
Resolution_Question: Make a new list called doubled that holds each number of [4, 5, 6] doubled, keeping the original as it was.

Incorrect_Code:
for i in len(items):
    print(items[i])  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Treats a number as something you can loop over, as if "for each of 5" were valid. `len()` returns a single integer, and a `for` loop needs an iterable such as `range(n)`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is len(items) a collection you can walk through, or a single value?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: len() returns one integer. A for loop needs an iterable, and range(n) turns a number into a sequence of values from 0 to n-1.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use `for i in range(len(items)):`, or just `for item in items:`.
Resolution_Question: Print the index and value of each item in colors = ["red", "blue"] using range(len(...)).

Incorrect_Code:
for n in nums:
    total = 0
    total += n
print(total)  # last item only
Correct_Code:
total = 0
for n in nums:
    total += n
print(total)
Underlying_Misconception: Doesn't see that the loop body runs from the top on every pass. Initialization placed inside the body resets the accumulator each time. The learner confuses code that sets up state with code that repeats.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many times does `total = 0` run if the loop goes over five numbers?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Everything in the loop body repeats on every pass. Setup code that should run once must go before the loop.
Resolution_Question: Write code that finds the largest number in nums without using max().

Incorrect_Code:
d = {"x": 1, "y": 2}
first = d.keys()[0]  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `.keys()` returns an indexable list. It returns a view object, which can be iterated and checked for membership but not indexed.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Can you pick an item from d.keys() with an index like [0]?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: keys() returns a view object. You can loop over it or test membership, but you cannot index it. Convert it to a list or use next(iter(...)).
Resolution_Question: Get the first value of the dict ages = {"A": 30, "B": 25}.

Incorrect_Code:
def reset(n):
    n = 0
x = 5
reset(x)
print(x)  # still 5
Correct_Code:
def reset(n):
    return 0
x = 5
x = reset(x)
print(x)  # 0
Underlying_Misconception: Believes a function parameter is the caller's variable itself, so assigning to it changes the original. A parameter is a new local name. Rebinding it inside the function never affects the caller's name.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Inside reset(), does n = 0 change x in the caller, or only the name n?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A parameter is a new local name pointing at the same value. Rebinding it inside the function does not touch the caller's variable.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Return the new value and assign it: `x = reset(x)`.
Resolution_Question: Write a function double(n) that returns twice its input, and use it to update a variable score.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks a method is just a function that happens to sit inside a class. When called on an instance, Python passes that instance as the first argument automatically, so the method must declare a parameter to receive it.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When you call Dog().bark(), what does Python pass to bark automatically?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Calling a method on an instance passes that instance as the first argument. The method must have a parameter, normally self, to receive it.
Resolution_Question: Fix this method signature inside a class: `def set_name(name):`.

Underlying_Misconception: Doesn't separate a local variable (which vanishes when `__init__` ends) from an attribute stored on the object. Only assignment through `self.` attaches data to the instance.
Hint_L1_Socratic: After __init__ finishes, where does the variable name live?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A plain variable inside a method disappears when the method ends. Only values stored with self. are kept on the object.
Resolution_Question: Write a class Book whose __init__ stores a title and an author on the object.

Underlying_Misconception: Treats exceptions as nuisances to silence instead of information. A bare `except` also hides unrelated bugs (even typos and Ctrl+C), so the learner should name the specific failure they expect.
Hint_L1_Socratic: If a typo caused an error inside this try block, would you ever find out?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A bare except catches every error and pass hides it. Catch the specific error you expect and handle it in a useful way.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use `except ValueError:` and print a helpful message instead of `pass`.
Resolution_Question: Ask for a number and print "Invalid number" only when the text cannot be converted to an int.

Incorrect_Code:
with open("log.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("new entry\n")  # wipes old log
Correct_Code:
with open("log.txt", "a") as f:
    f.write("new entry\n")
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `"w"` means "write more" to the file. Write mode truncates the file the moment it is opened, while append mode (`"a"`) adds to the end.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does opening a file in "w" mode do to its existing content?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Write mode empties the file as soon as it is opened. Append mode ("a") keeps existing content and adds to the end.
Resolution_Question: Add the line "done" to the end of notes.txt without losing what is already there.

Incorrect_Code:
f = open("data.txt")
print(f.read())
print(f.read())  # prints empty string
Correct_Code:
f = open("data.txt")
text = f.read()
print(text)
print(text)
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks a file object is the file's contents, like a string. It is a stream with a current position, so after one `read()` the position is at the end and a second read returns nothing.
Hint_L1_Socratic: After the first read(), where is the file's position?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A file object is a stream with a current position. read() moves it to the end, so a second read() returns an empty string.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Store the result once: `text = f.read()` and reuse text.
Resolution_Question: Read a file once and print both its length and its content.

Incorrect_Code:
score = 10
print("Score: " + score)  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Expects `+` to join text and numbers automatically, as `print("a", 5)` or some other languages do. Python doesn't convert types implicitly here, so the number must be converted or formatted into the string.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What types are on each side of the + in this line?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Python does not convert numbers to text when you use + with a string. You must convert the number or use an f-string.
Resolution_Question: Print "Total: 95" using the integer variable total = 95 in an f-string.

Underlying_Misconception: Believes recursion knows when to stop, as a math definition "obviously" does. Each call must reach a base case that returns without recursing, otherwise the calls never end.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When would fact(n) ever stop calling itself?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Every recursive function needs a base case that returns without calling itself again. Without it the calls continue until Python stops them.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `if n <= 1: return 1` before the recursive return.
Resolution_Question: Write a recursive function countdown(n) that prints n down to 1 and then stops.

Incorrect_Code:
s = "python"
first_four = s[0:3]  # "pyt"
Underlying_Misconception: Reads the slice end index as inclusive. In `s[a:b]` the stop index is excluded, so the slice has `b - a` items.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is the character at index 3 included in s[0:3]?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: In a slice s[a:b] the stop index is excluded, so you get b - a characters.
Resolution_Question: Which slice gives the last three letters of "python"?

Incorrect_Code:
mid = len(items) / 2
print(items[mid])  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Expects `/` to return a whole number when the division is exact. In Python 3 `/` always returns a float, and indexes must be integers, so floor division `//` is needed.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What type does / return in Python 3, even when the division is exact?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: / always returns a float, and list indexes must be integers. // does floor division and returns an int.
Resolution_Question: Find the middle item of a list with 7 elements using integer division.

Incorrect_Code:
t = (5)
print(type(t))  # int
Underlying_Misconception: Believes parentheses create a tuple. It is the comma that does, and parentheses around a single value just group it, as in math.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Which character makes a tuple: the parentheses or the comma?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A comma creates a tuple. Parentheses around one value are only grouping, as in maths.
Resolution_Question: Define a tuple that holds only the string "data".

Incorrect_Code:
seen = {}
seen.add(3)  # AttributeError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes empty braces make an empty set because non-empty braces like `{1, 2}` do. `{}` is reserved for an empty dict, so an empty set requires `set()`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What type of object does {} create?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Empty braces create an empty dict, not a set. An empty set must be created with set().
Resolution_Question: Create an empty set and an empty dict in two separate lines.

Incorrect_Code:
if 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3:
    print("equal")  # never prints
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks floats store decimal numbers exactly. They are binary approximations, so results of arithmetic can differ by tiny amounts and should be compared with a tolerance.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Can a computer store 0.1 exactly in binary?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Floats are binary approximations, so results of arithmetic can differ by a tiny amount. Compare them within a tolerance, not with ==.
Resolution_Question: Write a check that is True when 0.7 + 0.1 is close to 0.8.

Incorrect_Code:
# in a file named random.py
import random
print(random.randint(1, 6))  # AttributeError
Correct_Code:
# rename the file to dice.py
import random
print(random.randint(1, 6))
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `import random` always finds the standard library. Python searches the current folder first, so a learner's own file with the same name shadows the library module.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When you write import random, which file does Python find first?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Python searches the current folder before the standard library. A file named random.py shadows the real module.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Rename your file to something else, such as dice.py (and delete any leftover __pycache__).
Resolution_Question: Name three file names you should avoid because they match standard library modules.

Incorrect_Code:
class Cart:
    items = []
a, b = Cart(), Cart()
a.items.append("x")
print(b.items)  # ['x']
Underlying_Misconception: Confuses class-level attributes (one object shared by every instance) with instance attributes (created per object in `__init__`). A mutable class attribute is shared state.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is items stored once per Cart object, or once for the whole class?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: An attribute defined in the class body is shared by all instances. Per-object data must be created in __init__ with self.
Resolution_Question: Create a class Player where every player gets their own empty list of badges.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks consecutive `if` statements are linked, so a later one runs only when the earlier one failed. Each `if` is evaluated independently, and `elif` is what makes the branches mutually exclusive.
Hint_L1_Socratic: If score is 95, how many of the if statements are checked?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Each separate if is tested independently. elif only runs when the earlier conditions were False.
Resolution_Question: Write grade logic with if / elif / else for 90+, 80+ and anything lower.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks the loop variable of a `for` loop is a position. It is the element itself, so using it as an index fails. Getting both position and element needs `enumerate()`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: In `for i in fruits`, is i a position or a fruit?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: The loop variable is the element itself, not its index. enumerate() gives both position and element.
Resolution_Question: Print each color of colors = ["red", "blue"] with its position number starting at 1.

Incorrect_Code:
for i in range(5, 0):
    print(i)  # prints nothing
Underlying_Misconception: Expects `range` to work out the direction on its own. The default step is +1, so a start larger than the stop gives an empty sequence unless a negative step is given.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Which direction does range(5, 0) move, and what is the default step?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: The default step is +1, so a start larger than the stop gives an empty sequence. Counting down needs a negative step.
Resolution_Question: Print the even numbers from 10 down to 2.

Incorrect_Code:
sq = (n * n for n in nums)
print(sum(sq))
print(sum(sq))  # 0
Correct_Code:
sq = [n * n for n in nums]
print(sum(sq))
print(sum(sq))
Underlying_Misconception: Treats a generator expression like a stored list. A generator is a one-shot iterator that produces values on demand, so once consumed it is empty.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What is left in the generator after sum(sq) has used it once?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A generator produces values once. After it has been consumed it is empty, unlike a list.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use square brackets to build a list: `sq = [n * n for n in nums]`.
Resolution_Question: Explain why you can loop over a list twice but over a generator only once, and show it in code.

Incorrect_Code:
pairs = zip(a, b)
print(len(pairs))  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `zip` builds a list. It returns a lazy iterator with no length and no indexing, so it must be converted with `list()` or consumed in a loop.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does zip give you a list, or something else?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: zip returns a lazy iterator. It has no length and no indexing until you convert it with list().
Resolution_Question: Combine names and ages into pairs and print how many there are.

Incorrect_Code:
d = {"x": 9, "y": 3}
best = max(d)  # "y"
Underlying_Misconception: Forgets that iterating a dict yields keys, so `max(d)` compares the keys alphabetically. Finding the key with the biggest value requires telling `max` what to compare.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does max(d) compare when d is a dict?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Looping over a dict gives keys, so max compares the keys. The key argument tells max what to compare instead.
Resolution_Question: Find the name with the lowest score in scores = {"Ana": 90, "Raj": 85}.

Incorrect_Code:
import math
print(sqrt(16))  # NameError
Underlying_Misconception: Believes importing a module drops its contents into the current namespace. `import math` only binds the name `math`, so its functions are reached through it.
Hint_L1_Socratic: After import math, which name has been added to your program?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: import math adds only the name math. Its functions are reached through it, as math.sqrt.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Write `math.sqrt(16)`, or use `from math import sqrt`.
Resolution_Question: Print the value of pi using the math module.

Underlying_Misconception: Treats `find` as a yes/no test. It returns an index (0 here, which is falsy) or -1 when absent (which is truthy), so the check is both wrong and inverted.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does find return when the letter is at the very start, and what does it return when the letter is missing?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: find returns an index, and 0 is falsy while -1 is truthy. It is a position search, not a yes/no test.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use the in operator: `if "h" in s:`.
Resolution_Question: Check whether "@" appears in the string email.

Underlying_Misconception: Equates "falsy" with "absent". Valid values such as `0`, `""` and `[]` are also falsy, so an existence check must test for `None` specifically.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is 0 the same as "no value"?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: 0, "", [] and None are all falsy, but only None means nothing was given. To test for absence, check for None directly.
Resolution_Question: Write a function that prints "missing" only when its argument is None, not when it is 0.

Correct_Code:
import copy
a = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
b = copy.deepcopy(a)
b[0][0] = 99
print(a[0][0])  # 1
Underlying_Misconception: Believes `.copy()` duplicates everything. It copies only the outer list, so the inner lists are still shared. Nested structures need a deep copy.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does .copy() copy the lists inside the list too?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: .copy() makes a shallow copy. The outer list is new, but the inner lists are still shared. copy.deepcopy copies everything.
Resolution_Question: Copy a list of lists so that changing the copy's first inner list leaves the original untouched.

Correct_Code:
def counter():
    n = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return inc
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks an inner function can reassign a variable of the enclosing function. Assignment makes the name local to `inc`, so rebinding the outer variable must be declared with `nonlocal`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does `n += 1` inside inc() change the n from counter(), or create a new local one?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Assigning inside the inner function makes n local to it. nonlocal tells Python the name belongs to the enclosing function.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `nonlocal n` as the first line of inc().
Resolution_Question: Write a closure make_adder_counter() that returns a function increasing a stored total by 5 on each call.

Underlying_Misconception: Imagines a function can return several separate values. It returns one tuple, so the caller must unpack it or index into it.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many values does minmax really return?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A function returns one object. Returning two values creates a tuple, which the caller must unpack or index.
Resolution_Question: Write a function that returns the first and last items of a list, and store them in two variables.

Underlying_Misconception: Expects `append` to add every item of what it is given. It adds exactly one element, here the whole list as a single nested item, while `extend` adds the items one by one.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many items does append add to the list?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: append adds exactly one element, even if it is itself a list. extend adds each item of an iterable one by one.
Resolution_Question: Join [1, 2] and [3, 4] into one flat list in two different ways.

Correct_Code:
d = {"a": 1, "b": 2}
d = {k: v for k, v in d.items() if v != 1}
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes a dict can be edited while it is being looped over. Changing its size during iteration invalidates the iterator, so build a new dict or loop over a copy of the keys.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What happens to a dict's size while a loop is still reading it?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Changing the size of a dict while iterating invalidates the loop. Build a new dict or loop over a copy.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Create a new dict with a comprehension, or loop over `list(d)`.
Resolution_Question: Remove all items with a value of 0 from stock = {"a": 0, "b": 4}.

Incorrect_Code: print("10" < "9")  # True
Underlying_Misconception: Reads digit strings as numbers when comparing. Strings compare character by character, so `"1"` comes before `"9"` and the result is the opposite of the numeric one.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does Python compare "10" and "9" as numbers or as text?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Strings compare character by character, so "1" comes before "9" and "10" is smaller. Convert to int to compare numbers.
Resolution_Question: Sort the strings ["10", "9", "100"] in numeric order.

Incorrect_Code: print(round(2.5))  # 2
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `round` always rounds halves up, as taught in school. Python uses round-half-to-even, so `round(2.5)` is 2 and `round(3.5)` is 4. The fix shown works for positive numbers only.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does round(2.5) return, and what about round(3.5)?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Python rounds halves to the nearest even number (banker's rounding), so 2.5 becomes 2. Always rounding up needs a different method.
Resolution_Question: Round 0.5, 1.5 and 2.5 and explain the pattern you see.

Incorrect_Code:
name = "  ada "
name.strip()
print(name)  # still padded
Underlying_Misconception: Expects a string method to change the variable it was called on. Strings are immutable, so the method returns a new string, and that result is lost unless it is assigned to a name.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does strip() change name, or does it give you something back?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Strings are immutable, so string methods return a new string. If you do not store it, it is lost.
Resolution_Question: Convert "  Hello " to lowercase with no spaces around it and print it.

Incorrect_Code:
if input("Age: ") == 18:  # never True
    print("adult")
Underlying_Misconception: Treats the text "18" and the number 18 as the same thing because they look alike when printed. `input()` returns a string, and a string never equals an int in Python.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What type is the value returned by input(), and what type is 18?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: input() returns a string, and a string is never equal to an int, even if they look the same when printed.
Resolution_Question: Ask for a number and print "even" if it is even.

Incorrect_Code: print "hello"  # SyntaxError
Underlying_Misconception: Carries over syntax from old tutorials, where print was a statement. In Python 3 `print` is an ordinary function, so it must be called with parentheses.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is print a statement or a function in Python 3?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: In Python 3 print is a function, so its arguments go inside parentheses.
Resolution_Question: Print the sentence "Hello, world" on one line and the number 42 on the next.

Incorrect_Code:
if x > 3
    print(x)  # SyntaxError
Underlying_Misconception: Treats the colon as optional punctuation. It marks the start of a block, and Python needs it to know that an indented body follows the header.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What symbol tells Python that an indented block follows?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A colon at the end of a header line marks the start of a block. Without it, Python cannot tell the line is a header.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `:` at the end of the if line.
Resolution_Question: Fix the header: `while count < 3`.

Incorrect_Code:
def greet():
print("hi")  # IndentationError
Underlying_Misconception: Sees indentation as formatting for readability. In Python it is syntax that defines which statements belong to a function, loop or condition.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What line should belong inside greet(), and how does Python know?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Indentation is part of Python's syntax. It shows which statements belong to a function, loop or condition.
Resolution_Question: Fix the indentation in: `for i in range(3):` followed by `print(i)` on the next line.

Underlying_Misconception: Reads a loop's `else` as the else of the inner `if`. It belongs to the loop and runs only when the loop finishes without hitting `break`, so without `break` it always runs.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Which statement does that else belong to: the if or the for?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A loop's else runs when the loop ends without a break. Without a break, it runs every time.
Resolution_Question: Write a loop that searches a list and prints "missing" only if the item is not found.

Underlying_Misconception: Mixes up leaving the loop with skipping one pass. `break` ends the loop entirely, while `continue` jumps to the next iteration.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What is the difference between leaving a loop and skipping to its next pass?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: break ends the whole loop. continue skips the rest of the current pass and moves on to the next item.
Resolution_Question: Print only the positive numbers from [3, -1, 4, -5, 2] without stopping early.

Incorrect_Code:
if x > 0 and < 10:  # SyntaxError
    print("ok")
Underlying_Misconception: Drops the repeated subject, as in the English phrase "x is above 0 and below 10". Python needs a complete comparison on each side of `and`, or the chained form `0 < x < 10`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does Python need on each side of `and`?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Each side of and must be a complete expression. Python also lets you chain comparisons as 0 < x < 10.
Resolution_Question: Write a condition that is True when age is between 18 and 65 inclusive.

Incorrect_Code: print(-7 // 2)  # -4, expected -3
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes integer division cuts off the decimals. `//` is floor division, which rounds toward negative infinity, so negative results come out one lower than truncation would give.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does // cut off decimals, or round in a particular direction?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: // is floor division and rounds toward negative infinity. For -3.5 that gives -4, not -3.
Resolution_Question: Calculate -9 // 4 by hand and check it in Python.

Incorrect_Code:
a = b
b = a  # both now hold b's old value
Underlying_Misconception: Believes assignments happen "at the same time" like a mathematical swap. They run one after another, so the first line overwrites `a` and its old value is lost before it can be copied.
Hint_L1_Socratic: After the first line a = b runs, what happened to a's old value?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Assignments run one after the other. The first line overwrites a before its old value is saved.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use tuple swap: `a, b = b, a`.
Resolution_Question: Swap the values of first and second without using a third variable.

Incorrect_Code: ,.join([1, 2, 3])  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Expects `join` to convert items to text as `print` does. It only accepts strings, so each item must be converted first.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What type of items does join accept?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: join only works on strings. Numbers must be converted first.
Resolution_Question: Join the numbers [4, 5, 6] into the text "4-5-6".

Incorrect_Code: pos = nums.index(9)  # ValueError if 9 is absent
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes a failed search returns a sentinel such as -1, like `str.find` does. `list.index` raises `ValueError` when the item is missing, so presence must be checked first.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What happens when index() cannot find the item?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: list.index raises ValueError if the item is not there. Check with `in` first, or use try/except.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Write `if 9 in nums:` before calling nums.index(9).
Resolution_Question: Return the position of x in a list, or -1 if it is not present.

Incorrect_Code:
nums = [10, 20, 30]
nums.remove(2)  # ValueError
Underlying_Misconception: Reads `remove` as "remove at position". It removes the first item equal to the value given, so removing by position needs `del` or `pop`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does remove take a position or a value?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: remove deletes the first item equal to the value given. To delete by position, use del or pop.
Resolution_Question: Delete the first item of a list in two different ways.

Incorrect_Code: sorted([3, "a", 1])  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes any values can be ordered against each other. Python only compares values of compatible types, so a mixed list has to be converted to one type first.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Can Python decide whether 3 is bigger than "a"?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Sorting needs items that can be compared with each other. Numbers and strings cannot, so convert them to one type.
Resolution_Question: Sort the list [3, "a", 1] so all items are compared as text.

Incorrect_Code: sorted(words, key=len())  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Doesn't separate passing a function from calling it. `key` needs the function object itself so `sorted` can call it on each item. Writing `len()` calls it right away with no argument.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What is the difference between len and len() ?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: key expects a function object that sorted will call for each item. Writing len() calls it right now without an argument.
Resolution_Question: Sort a list of words by their last letter.

Incorrect_Code:
def f(a=1, b):  # SyntaxError
    return a + b
Correct_Code:
def f(b, a=1):
    return a + b
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks parameters can be listed in any order. Positional arguments are matched left to right, so every parameter after one with a default must have a default too.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Which parameters can be left out when calling f?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Parameters without defaults must come before those with defaults, so Python can match arguments from left to right.
Resolution_Question: Fix this signature: `def greet(greeting="Hi", name):`.

Underlying_Misconception: Assumes a function accepts any number of arguments and gathers them itself. The parameter list fixes how many are allowed, and `*nums` is what collects extras into a tuple.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many arguments does total(nums) accept?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A normal parameter takes one argument. *nums collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple.
Resolution_Question: Write a function that accepts any number of numbers and returns the largest.

Incorrect_Code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
pair = (2, 3)
add(pair)  # TypeError
Correct_Code:
def add(a, b):
    return a + b
pair = (2, 3)
add(*pair)
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks passing a tuple supplies its items as separate arguments. It is passed as one argument, and the `*` operator is needed to unpack it into several.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many arguments are you passing when you write add(pair)?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A tuple passed this way is one argument. The * operator unpacks it into separate arguments.
Resolution_Question: Call the function max_of(a, b, c) with the values stored in a list of 3 numbers.

Incorrect_Code:
if __name__ == "main":
    run()  # never runs
Underlying_Misconception: Treats this idiom as a magic phrase to memorize rather than a comparison. `__name__` is set to the exact string `"__main__"` when a file is run directly, so any other spelling is never true.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What exact string does __name__ hold when a file is run directly?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: __name__ is set to the string "__main__" with double underscores. Any other spelling never matches.
Resolution_Question: Explain what happens to code under this check when the file is imported by another file.

Incorrect_Code:
if input("Continue? ") == "Yes":
    go()  # fails for "yes"
Underlying_Misconception: Expects string comparison to behave as a person reads it. Python compares exact characters, so case and stray spaces matter, and user input should be normalised first.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Would "yes" or " Yes " match "Yes"?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: String comparison is exact, so capital letters and spaces matter. Clean the input before comparing.
Resolution_Question: Ask for a name and greet the user whether they type it in capitals or small letters.

Incorrect_Code: len(12345)  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks a number is a sequence of digits. An integer is a single value with no length, so counting digits means converting it to a string first.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does the number 12345 have a length?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: An int is one value, not a sequence of digits. To count digits, convert it to a string first.
Resolution_Question: Print how many digits are in the number n = 9081.

Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `in` searches everything inside a dict. For a dict it tests keys only, so searching values needs `.values()`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When you ask whether 3 is in a dict, which part of the dict is checked?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: `in` on a dict tests keys only. Use .values() to search values.
Resolution_Question: Check whether any student in grades = {"Ana": 90} scored 90.

Incorrect_Code:
words = ["hi", "yo", "hey"]
d = {len(w): w for w in words}  # {2: "yo", 3: "hey"}
Underlying_Misconception: Believes a dict key can hold several values by repeating it. Each key is unique, so a later entry silently replaces an earlier one. Grouping needs a list as the value.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What happens to the first entry when two words have the same length?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Dict keys are unique, so a later entry overwrites an earlier one. To keep several, store a list as the value.
Resolution_Question: Group the words ["cat", "dog", "bird"] by their first letter.

Incorrect_Code: avg = sum(nums) / len(nums)  # ZeroDivisionError if empty
Correct_Code: avg = sum(nums) / len(nums) if nums else 0
Underlying_Misconception: Writes code only for the typical case. An empty input is a valid case too, and the learner hasn't built the habit of asking what happens at the boundaries.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does len(nums) equal when the list is empty?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Empty input is a valid case. Dividing by zero raises an error, so handle the empty list first.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add a check: `... if nums else 0`.
Resolution_Question: Write a function that returns the average of a list, or None if the list is empty.

Incorrect_Code: int("3.7")  # ValueError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes `int()` can parse any number written as text and cut off the decimals. Applied to a string it accepts only whole-number text, so the string must go through `float` first.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Can int() read the text "3.7" directly?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: int() on a string accepts only whole-number text. A decimal string must go through float first.
Resolution_Question: Convert the text "12.9" to a whole number.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks converting the text "False" gives the boolean False. `bool()` on a string checks only whether it is empty, so every non-empty string is True.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is "False" an empty string?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: bool() on a string is False only when the string is empty. Any other text, including "False", is True.
Resolution_Question: Turn the text "yes" or "no" into a real boolean.

Incorrect_Code:
x = 5
x++  # SyntaxError
Underlying_Misconception: Carries over an increment operator from other languages. Python has no `++`, so adding one is written as an assignment with `+= 1`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does Python have a ++ operator?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Python has no ++ or --. Use += 1 to add one.
Resolution_Question: Write a loop that adds 1 to a counter until it reaches 5.

Incorrect_Code:
f = open("a.txt", "w")
f.write("hi")
print(open("a.txt").read())  # may be empty
Correct_Code:
with open("a.txt", "w") as f:
    f.write("hi")
print(open("a.txt").read())
Underlying_Misconception: Believes `write` puts data on disk immediately. Output is buffered and only guaranteed to be saved once the file is flushed or closed, so closing is part of the work.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When is data from write() guaranteed to be saved?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Written data is buffered and only guaranteed to be on disk after the file is flushed or closed. A with block closes it for you.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Wrap the code in `with open(...) as f:`.
Resolution_Question: Write two lines to out.txt and make sure they are saved before reading them back.

Incorrect_Code: open("C:\new\table.txt")  # \n and \t become characters
Underlying_Misconception: Treats the backslash as an ordinary character inside a string literal. It starts an escape sequence, so `\n` becomes a newline. A raw string (`r"..."`) or doubled backslashes are needed.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does \n mean inside a normal string?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A backslash starts an escape sequence, so \n becomes a newline and \t becomes a tab. Raw strings treat backslashes literally.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add an r before the quote: `r"C:\new\table.txt"`.
Resolution_Question: Write the path D:\temp\notes.txt safely in two different ways.

Incorrect_Code:
with open("a.txt") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
if lines[0] == "yes":  # item is "yes\n"
    go()
Correct_Code:
with open("a.txt") as f:
    lines = f.readlines()
if lines[0].strip() == "yes":
    go()
Underlying_Misconception: Doesn't realise each line read from a file keeps its trailing newline character. The text looks like "yes" when printed but is not equal to it.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does the line you read from the file include any invisible characters at the end?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: readlines() keeps the newline at the end of every line. The text looks the same when printed but is not equal.
Resolution_Question: Read a file and print its lines without extra blank lines.

Incorrect_Code:
name = "Ada"
print("Hello {name}")  # prints {name}
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks braces in any string are filled in automatically. Only a string with the `f` prefix evaluates the expressions inside the braces. Otherwise they are ordinary characters.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What turns a normal string into one that fills in {name}?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Only f-strings, which start with f before the quote, evaluate expressions inside braces.
Resolution_Question: Print "Ada is 20" using the variables name and age in an f-string.

Incorrect_Code: a, b = "1 2 3".split()  # ValueError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes unpacking takes as many items as it can. The number of names on the left must match the number of items exactly, or Python raises an error.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many items does split() give for "1 2 3", and how many names are on the left?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Unpacking needs the same number of names as items. A mismatch raises ValueError.
Resolution_Question: Unpack the text "x y" into two variables.

Incorrect_Code:
for i in range(1, 10):
    print(i)  # stops at 9
Underlying_Misconception: Reads the end value of `range` as inclusive, as in "1 to 10". The stop value is excluded, which is the same convention as in slicing.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is 10 included in range(1, 10)?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: The stop value of range is excluded, just like in slicing.
Resolution_Question: Print the numbers 1 to 20 inclusive.

Correct_Code:
for step in range(1, 11):
    x = step / 10
Underlying_Misconception: Expects repeated float addition to land exactly on a decimal target. Rounding errors build up, so the exact value is never reached. Loops should be driven by integers or use `<`.

Hint_L2_Conceptual: Floats cannot store 0.1 exactly, so errors build up and the exact target is skipped. Use integers to drive the loop.

Resolution_Question: Write a loop that prints 0.0, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5 and 2.0 without testing floats for equality.

Incorrect_Code:
t = (1, 2, 3)
t[0] = 9  # TypeError

Hint_L1_Socratic: Can you change an item of a tuple after it is created?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Tuples are immutable. To change one, build a new tuple or use a list from the start.
Resolution_Question: Change the middle value of (1, 2, 3) to 5 without a list.

Incorrect_Code:
s = {3, 1, 2}
print(s[0])  # TypeError

Hint_L1_Socratic: Do the items in a set have positions?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Sets are unordered, so they have no indexes. Use sorted() or a list when order matters.
Resolution_Question: Print the smallest item of a set.

Incorrect_Code:
s = "abc"
s = s.reverse()  # AttributeError
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes every sequence type shares the same methods. `reverse()` exists only on lists, and a string is reversed by slicing with a negative step.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does a string have a reverse method?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: reverse() exists on lists only. Strings are reversed with the slice [::-1] or reversed().
Resolution_Question: Check whether a word is a palindrome.

Underlying_Misconception: Makes the print-versus-return mistake again, inside a special method. `__str__` must hand back a string for Python to display, not print one itself.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What must __str__ hand back to Python?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: __str__ must return a string. Printing inside it shows text but returns None, which Python rejects.
Resolution_Question: Add a __str__ method to a class Car that returns "Car: <brand>".

Underlying_Misconception: Assumes two objects with equal contents are equal. By default `==` compares identity, so a class must define `__eq__` to say what equality means for it.

Hint_L2_Conceptual: By default == compares identity, not contents. A class must define __eq__ to say when two objects are equal.
Resolution_Question: Make two Money objects equal when their amounts are equal.

Underlying_Misconception: Confuses the class with an instance of it. Without parentheses `d` is just another name for the class, and a method needing `self` has no object to work on.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What is the difference between Dog and Dog()?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Dog is the class itself. Dog() creates an instance, and only an instance can supply self to a method.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks `*nums` means "give me a list". It collects separate positional arguments into a tuple, so passing one list produces a tuple holding a single list. To spread a list into separate arguments at the call, it must be unpacked with `*`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: How many arguments does total([1, 2, 3]) receive, and what does nums contain inside the function?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: *nums gathers each positional argument into a tuple. One list argument becomes a tuple with one item (the list). Putting * before a list at the call site spreads its items out as separate arguments.
Resolution_Question: Write a function show_all(*items) that prints each item, then call it with the list ["a", "b", "c"] without changing the function.

Underlying_Misconception: Believes `**opts` accepts a dict as an ordinary argument. It collects keyword arguments (name=value) into a dict, so a dict passed positionally is rejected. It must be unpacked with `**` at the call.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is {"a": 1} passed as a keyword argument or as a positional one?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: **opts gathers name=value arguments into a dict. A dict given as a plain positional argument has no name, so Python has nowhere to put it. ** at the call spreads a dict into keyword arguments.
Resolution_Question: Given settings = {"color": "red", "size": 3}, call a function describe(**kwargs) so that it receives both settings.

Underlying_Misconception: Treats a function placed inside a class as if it were an ordinary function. Called on an instance, it receives the instance as an extra first argument. A method that does not need the instance must be marked `@staticmethod` (or take `self`).
Hint_L1_Socratic: When you call Calc().add(2, 3), how many arguments does Python actually pass to add?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Calling a method through an instance passes that instance first, so add receives three arguments. @staticmethod tells Python not to pass the instance.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `@staticmethod` on the line above `def add(a, b):`.
Resolution_Question: Write a class MathTools with a static method double(n) that returns n * 2, and call it using the class name instead of an instance.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks every method must be called with parentheses. `@property` turns a method into an attribute that is computed on access, so `.area` already returns the number and the extra `()` tries to call a float.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does Circle(2).area give back before you add the parentheses?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A property runs its method when you read the attribute and returns the result. Adding () then tries to call that returned float, which fails.
Resolution_Question: Add a property diameter to Circle that returns twice the radius, and print it for Circle(5).

Underlying_Misconception: Assumes a subclass's `__init__` automatically runs the parent's `__init__` too. Defining `__init__` in the subclass replaces the inherited one, so the parent's setup runs only if the subclass calls `super().__init__()`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Which __init__ runs when you create Dog("Rex", "Lab"), and does it ever set self.name?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: A method defined in the subclass overrides the parent's version. The parent's __init__ is not called unless you call it yourself with super().
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `super().__init__(name)` as the first line of Dog.__init__.
Resolution_Question: Write a class Cat that inherits from Animal, adds a color attribute, and still stores the name.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks `type(x) == Class` asks "is x a kind of Class". It asks for the exact class only, so instances of subclasses fail the test. `isinstance` also accepts subclasses.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Is a Dog exactly an Animal, or a kind of Animal? Which one does type(d) == Animal test?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: type() returns the exact class and == compares it exactly. isinstance(obj, Class) is True for that class and for any of its subclasses.
Resolution_Question: Write a check that is True when value is an int or a float, using a single isinstance call.

Incorrect_Code: raise "Something went wrong"  # TypeError
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks any message can be raised like a note. Only exception objects (instances of classes derived from `BaseException`) can be raised, and the message goes inside one of them as an argument.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What kind of object does `raise` expect after it: a string or an exception?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: raise needs an exception class or instance, such as ValueError or RuntimeError. The text is passed to it as an argument.
Resolution_Question: Write a function set_age(age) that raises a ValueError with a clear message when age is negative.

Underlying_Misconception: Assumes Python picks the best-matching `except` block. It checks them from top to bottom and runs the first one that matches, so a broad `Exception` listed first catches everything and the specific block below it is unreachable.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When int("x") fails, which except line does Python check first, and does it match?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: except blocks are tested in order and only the first match runs. ValueError is a kind of Exception, so Exception matches first. Put specific errors before general ones.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Swap the blocks so `except ValueError:` comes before `except Exception:`.
Resolution_Question: Write a try block around int(text) that handles ValueError with one message and any other exception with a different message.

Underlying_Misconception: Believes the name after `as` stays available after the except block. Python deletes it when the block ends, so the error text must be copied to another variable inside the block.
Hint_L1_Socratic: After the except block finishes, does the name e still exist?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: The variable bound by `as e` is removed automatically at the end of the except block. To keep the information, store it in another name inside the block.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Inside the block write `message = str(e)` and use message later.
Resolution_Question: Catch the error from int("abc") and keep its text in a variable that you can print after the try statement.

Incorrect_Code:
words = list("hello world")
print(words)  # single characters, not words
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks `list()` splits text into words. Calling list on a string breaks it into individual characters, because a string is a sequence of characters. Splitting into words needs `.split()`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: When you iterate over a string, what does each step give you?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: list(s) walks through s one character at a time, spaces included. split() cuts the string at whitespace (or any separator you give) and returns the pieces.
Resolution_Question: Turn "red,green,blue" into a list of three colors.

Underlying_Misconception: Expects `all()` to be False when there is nothing to check. With no items, no item fails the test, so `all([])` is True (a vacuous truth). An emptiness check has to be added separately.
Hint_L1_Socratic: If there are no scores, is there any score that fails the test?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: all() is True unless it finds an item that fails. An empty collection has none, so the result is True. Guard against it if "nobody" should not count as success.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Add `scores and` before the all(...) call.
Resolution_Question: Write a check that prints "all positive" only when nums is non-empty and every number is above 0.

Incorrect_Code:
from collections import defaultdict
d = defaultdict(int)
if d["a"] == 0:

print(len(d))  # 1, reading created the key
Correct_Code:
from collections import defaultdict
d = defaultdict(int)
if d.get("a", 0) == 0:

print(len(d))  # 0
Underlying_Misconception: Thinks reading from a `defaultdict` is harmless. Looking up a missing key with square brackets calls the factory and stores the new entry, so merely checking a value changes the dict. `.get()` and `in` do not.

Hint_L2_Conceptual: A defaultdict creates and stores a default value whenever a missing key is accessed with []. To only look, use `key in d` or `d.get(key)`.
Resolution_Question: Count how many times each letter appears in "hello" with a defaultdict(int), then check the letter "z" without adding it to the dict.

Incorrect_Code:
items = ["a", "b", "c"]
last = items[-0]  # "a", not "c"
Underlying_Misconception: Treats the minus sign as "from the end" for any number. Negative indexes count backwards starting at -1, and -0 is just 0, so it gives the first item.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What number is -0 in Python, and which item has that index?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Counting from the end begins at -1 (last item), -2 (second to last), and so on. Since -0 equals 0, items[-0] is the first item.
Resolution_Question: Print the second-to-last item of colors = ["red", "green", "blue", "pink"].

Incorrect_Code:
a, b = input("Two numbers: ").split()  # user types: 3 4
print(a + b)  # "34"
Correct_Code:
a, b = map(int, input("Two numbers: ").split())  # user types: 3 4
print(a + b)  # 7
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes pieces taken from text are numbers because they look like digits. `split()` returns strings, so `+` joins them. Each piece must be converted, often with `map(int, ...)`.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What type is each piece that split() returns when the user types 3 4?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: split() cuts text into a list of strings, and + on two strings concatenates them. Convert every piece with int() before doing arithmetic.
Resolution_Question: Read three numbers typed on one line and print their total.

Incorrect_Code:

Correct_Code:
for i in range(3):

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks each print continues on the same line. print ends every call with a newline by default, and the `end` argument sets what is written instead.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What does print add after the text each time it runs?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: By default print ends every call with a newline character. end= replaces it, for example with a space or an empty string.
Resolution_Question: Print the numbers 1 to 5 on a single line separated by single spaces.

Incorrect_Code:

Underlying_Misconception: Assumes the max of nothing is 0 or `None`. max and min need at least one item and raise ValueError on an empty collection, unless a `default=` value is supplied.
Hint_L1_Socratic: Which value should be the biggest of zero values?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: There is no sensible maximum of an empty sequence, so Python raises ValueError. The default= argument gives a value to return instead.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use `max(scores, default=None)`, or check `if scores:` first.
Resolution_Question: Find the smallest number in nums and give 0 when nums is empty.

Hint_L2_Conceptual: pop(i) removes the item at index i. remove(x) removes the first item equal to x. Index 20 does not exist in a three-item list.
Resolution_Question: From letters = ["a", "b", "c"], remove "b" one way and remove the last item another way.

Underlying_Misconception: Expects `+` to combine any collection. Sets do not support `+`. Their combination is union, written `|` or `.union()`, because set operators describe set logic and not list-style joining.
Hint_L1_Socratic: What should a + b do with the 2 that is in both sets, since a set cannot hold duplicates?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Sets use operators for set logic: | for union, & for intersection, - for difference. + is not defined for them.
Resolution_Question: Find the items that two sets have in common: set_a = {1, 2, 3} and set_b = {2, 3, 4}.

Incorrect_Code:

unique = list(set(names))  # order is not guaranteed
Underlying_Misconception: Assumes a set remembers insertion order. Sets are unordered, so converting to a set removes duplicates but may scramble the order. Dict keys are unique and keep insertion order (Python 3.7+).
Hint_L1_Socratic: Does a set promise to keep items in the order you added them?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Sets are unordered collections. dict.fromkeys(names) builds a dict whose keys are unique and keep first-seen order, so listing it gives order-preserving de-duplication.

Hint_L2_Conceptual: Methods that modify a list in place return None. Use the reverse=True option of sorted() to get a new descending list in one step.
Resolution_Question: Get a new list of words = ["pear", "fig", "apple"] sorted from Z to A.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks sorting text is alphabetical like a dictionary. Python compares strings by character code, where every capital letter comes before every lowercase letter. A key function can compare lowercase versions instead.
Hint_L1_Socratic: In character codes, does "C" come before or after "a"?
Hint_L2_Conceptual: Strings are compared by code point, so uppercase letters sort ahead of lowercase ones. Passing key=str.lower sorts as if everything were lowercase while keeping the original text.

Incorrect_Code:

Correct_Code:

Hint_L2_Conceptual: The "s" in loads stands for string. It parses JSON text. To read a file, open it and pass the file object to json.load.

Hint_L2_Conceptual: JSON allows only string keys. dumps turns 1 into "1", and loads gives back the string "1", not the int 1.

Resolution_Question: Round-trip {2: "b"} through JSON and print the type of its key.

Underlying_Misconception: Thinks `in` always means "contained inside". On a list it tests whether an item equals the value exactly. Only on a string does it test for a substring.

Hint_L2_Conceptual: For a list, in compares against each whole item. To look inside each string, check every item with any() and a string `in`.
Hint_L3_Targeted: Use `any("app" in w for w in words)`.
Resolution_Question: Check whether any word in names starts with "A".

Underlying_Misconception: Reads `.2` as "two decimal places". Without the `f` type it means two significant digits. The `f` makes it fixed-point notation with that many digits after the decimal point.
